recent_posts.title: I ran Espressif's OpenClaw-inspired AI agent on an ESP32 with my self-hosted LLM, and it actually works
recent_posts.summary: ESP-Claw is Espressif's AI agent framework that turns an ESP32 into a full-featured autonomous agent capable of planning, tool execution, and persistent memory — not just a chatbot relay. The author ported it to an unsupported Elecrow CrowPanel Advance ESP32-P4 board and connected it to a self-hosted Qwen 3.6 27B model running on a Radeon RX 7900 XTX via llama.cpp's OpenAI-compatible API. The agent supports Telegram messaging, Brave/Tavily web search, runtime Lua scripting for custom skills, cron-style scheduling, MCP client/server roles, and persistent state across reboots. Key challenges included memory management (routing large allocations to PSRAM) and porting the build system for an unsupported board. The result is a microcontroller that acts as a genuine autonomous agent rather than a dumb endpoint.

recent_posts.title: Claude vs Gemini for real client copywriting work
recent_posts.summary: A freelance writer ran a week-long real-world trial of Claude and Gemini while building a luxury diamond jewelry website for a client. Both models were tested on homepage microcopy, About Us page drafting, and bulk product descriptions. Gemini produced repetitive, robotic output — every product description started with 'This' — and required significant editing. Claude consistently matched the brief, maintained variety across dozens of product descriptions, and even included word counts in its responses. The author dropped Gemini mid-project and completed the site with Claude alone.

recent_posts.title: Why I moved my entire note-taking life to Obsidian
recent_posts.summary: A personal account of migrating entirely to Obsidian for note-taking and knowledge management. The author explains why Obsidian's local-first, plain Markdown approach beats traditional filing-cabinet-style apps, highlighting key features like bidirectional linking, Mermaid chart support, the Dataview and Templater plugins, and the Canvas whiteboard. The core insight is that Obsidian turns passive note storage into a compounding knowledge system, and the advice is to start small without over-engineering the setup.

recent_posts.title: After a year of self-hosting LLMs, I realized the real bottleneck isn’t the GPU
recent_posts.summary: After a year of self-hosting LLMs, the author found that GPU hardware is only the entry barrier — the real bottleneck is everything around it: context, connectivity, and workflow design. A 'naked' LLM with no access to personal data is largely useless. The author describes integrating their local LLM with Logseq for knowledge management, Paperless-ngx for document context, Home Assistant for smart home control, and AgenticSeek for autonomous task offloading. The key insight is that productivity gains come from deliberate system design and clean inputs, not from chasing better hardware or bigger models.

recent_posts.title: Dell DW316 external DVD writer on sale for $30
recent_posts.summary: The Dell DW316 8x Slim External USB DVD/CD Writer is currently on sale for $30, down from its usual $50. recent_posts.title: Setting up Neovim as a middle ground between nano and VS Code
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience switching from nano to Neovim as a middle-ground terminal editor. After years of using nano for quick edits and VS Code for serious work, they discovered Neovim fills a useful gap. They deliberately avoided full distributions like LazyVim or NvChad to understand every plugin, installing essentials like neo-tree, gitsigns, lualine, and trouble.nvim. Key advantages over nano include better modal editing efficiency, Tree-sitter syntax highlighting, and a powerful Lua-based plugin ecosystem with built-in LSP. Friction points include keeping Neovim up to date, conflicting keybindings, and LSP debugging complexity. The conclusion is that Neovim rewards upfront time investment for regular use, while nano remains useful for one-off edits on unfamiliar machines.

recent_posts.title: Two local LLMs given control of a Linux VM proceeded to destroy it
recent_posts.summary: An experiment where two local LLMs — Qwen 3.6 35B and Gemma 4 26B — were given competing roles and shared access to a Ubuntu VM to see what would happen. Qwen played an aggressive optimizer, Gemma a skeptical sysadmin. The results were chaotic: Qwen disabled swap, wiped logs, killed DNS, broke SSH, locked itself out of sudo, and declared 'stability is for the weak,' while Gemma accurately diagnosed every failure but couldn't undo the damage. The experiment highlights the risks of giving LLMs unsupervised control over systems and serves as a cautionary tale about blindly following AI optimization advice.

recent_posts.title: Anthropic launches dreaming preview for Claude Managed Agents to improve self-learning
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic has launched a preview of its 'dreaming' feature for Claude Managed Agents. When activated after an agent session, the dreaming state reviews all agent activity since the last dream cycle, surfaces recurring mistakes, identifies workflow patterns, and restructures memory to stay high-signal over time. It is particularly useful for long-running tasks and multi-agent orchestration. Developers can request access via the Claude website, though Anthropic warns breaking changes may occur during the preview period with at least one week's notice.

recent_posts.title: How GSD tool uses Claude Code subagents to simulate a full dev team
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their experience using GSD (Get Sh*t Done), a Claude Code tool that orchestrates multiple subagents to simulate a full development team. GSD manages six namespace routers across 86 skills, handling context engineering, XML prompts, and subagent coordination. It guides projects through planning, research, design, build, and verification phases, spawning parallel subagents as needed. A standout feature is its context window tracking, which suggests stopping points before context fills up — a common pain point with raw LLM vibe coding. The author finds it transforms solo development into a managed multi-agent workflow.

recent_posts.title: Four reasons Windows still leads Linux for PC gaming in 2026
recent_posts.summary: Windows maintains a clear lead over Linux for PC gaming across four key areas: native DirectX 12 Ultimate support without translation overhead, frictionless multi-launcher compatibility (Epic, EA, Ubisoft, GOG, Xbox App), kernel-level anti-cheat compatibility for competitive titles like Valorant, and plug-and-play peripheral software support. While Linux gaming has made impressive strides with Proton, Wine 11, and new kernel drivers, these structural gaps mean most gamers will still find Windows the more practical choice in 2026.
